subtitulo: Building an opinion that survives being questioned
descripcion: At C1 the problem is no longer *how* to say what you think but how to say it so that it holds. A C1 opinion has three parts a B1 opinion doesn't: a stated position, a reason that isn't a restatement of the position, and an acknowledged limit. Most learners produce the first, skip the second and never reach the third — which is why their opinions sound firm but empty. The other half of the skill is eliciting: pulling a real opinion out of someone who is being polite or vague.

ejemplos.texto: *My position is that hybrid work only fails where management was already weak — the office was covering for the problem, not solving it.*
*I'd distinguish between two things: whether it works, and whether people like it.*
*Where I'd stop short is claiming this applies to every role.*
*Is that a hunch, or have you actually seen it happen?*

notas: *I think* isn't weak, but it's cheap. Rotate through the framing column instead of repeating it.
*I'd distinguish between X and Y* is the highest-value move here: it signals you've thought about the question rather than reacted to it.
Naming the limit of your own claim strengthens it. Counter-intuitive, but reliably true in English argument.
errores: Circular reasoning: *I think remote work is good because working remotely is beneficial.*
*In my humble opinion* — reads as sarcastic to native ears. Avoid entirely.
*According to me* — not English. Use *in my view*.
Over-reliance on *for me*, which frames a judgement as a mere preference.

mision.consigna: State and defend a position on something contested at your workplace, in front of an imagined sceptic.

microtareas.texto: Write one opinion about your job three times: to a friend, to your manager, in a report.
Ask a colleague a real question using an eliciting phrase. Did you get a real answer or a polite one?
Record 90 seconds: *Should engineers be involved in commercial decisions?* Include one distinction.

autochequeo: Is my reason different from my position, or just a restatement?
Did I name one limit of my own claim?
Three different framing expressions, or *I think* three times?
Is my distinction a real distinction, or two words for the same thing?
All four core items — count them.
promptCorreccion: Focus only on how I express opinions. (1) Mark each framing device and say if it fits the register. (2) Point out any circular reasoning. (3) Is my distinction real or just two words for the same thing? (4) Rewrite my three weakest sentences. Do not rewrite the whole text — I want to see my own errors.

filas: *I'd say* → *My sense is* → *My position is* → *I'd argue*
supplies the reason, not a restatement
*because* → *the reason being* → *what makes me say that is*
splits a question others treat as one
*I'd separate two things* / *I'd distinguish between X and Y*
*Where I'd stop short is* / *I wouldn't extend it to*
That's my instinct, not my evidence
*What's your read?* → *Where do you land?* → *Is that a hunch or have you seen it?*
*You'd know better than me* / *I'm outside my lane*

contraste.es: Spanish can hedge inside the verb (*creo que sea* vs. *creo que es*); English can't. *I think* is only a frame, never a hedge, so English needs a second device stacked on top of it to soften anything.
